139.s: Talk of licences for cutting hair, his chickens, and learning to kill chickens at the restaurant.
139.q: I got about five or six guys in my block I'll cut the hair. But they don't know how I do it, you know how I'll write, you know what? You got to get a license, license ball to cut hair.

139.s: Talk of puppies chewing shirts, the dog that comes for supper at six, and dog chow.
139.q: Yeah. I'd get to step from on the floor. And he used to sleep right after putting a day with him. That's how he slept with him. That's right. That's right. Sings a character.

139.s: Talk of the shepherd-collie puppy, giving it bones, rubber chew toys and feeding schedules.
139.q: And this dog, I got you, he's a little puppy, but he don't chew his food at all. If you put something on your arm, gone. That's gone.

773.s: How people were insured without knowing, Miss Cole's role, and how insurance rules changed.
773.q: You know, she had, they say she used to insure so many people. And so she didn't insure them, they died. So that got so now that somehow or another like that, they say they didn't want her, you know, they stopped. That's how, I think she was the cause, they said they made that law that, you…

773.t: Playing the lottery in the Depression
773.s: She won on lottery numbers when her husband's eyes were bad.
773.q: And the children would get ready. Mm-hmm .

881.t: Losing the bag and ten years peddling vegetables
881.s: After leaving the post office he went broke, bought a truck and sold produce for about ten years.
881.q: It wasn't high. What year was that in? Well, it was, it must have been in the, in the early, it was, it was after the war, because I came down here in 46. Yeah. And I must have started after 46. And so I could see I was getting broke, you know, and I started to gamble too. And so I said, well, if I…

881.t: Selling Christmas trees and rotten fish
881.s: Stories of buying produce, Christmas trees and a load of bad fish.
881.q: And I used to sell Christmas trees. See, I'd sell somewhere around two or three thousand Christmas trees. And when everybody else was busted on Christmas day, I'm sitting there with eight or nine hundred dollars. See? I'd go out there, a lot of times I'd look and go out there in the freight yards.…

175.t: Fish fry setting and scrubbing steps with red brick
175.s: Fish fries were mostly indoors in Prohibition days; the red brick and Gold Dust-style powder used to scrub steps are described.
175.q: No, well, depending on how the weather was. But most of the fish fries that I had been to was more or less the inside. Inside? Yeah. You'd go over there and you'd buy fish and you could eat it there, you could even take it out. And of course that was during the prohibition days too, you could…

863.t: The craft of cutting and hanging paper ceilings
863.s: He describes cutting paper with a razor, hanging it in rotation, working with Brother Fortuny, and picking up the skill without training.
863.q: You have to cut it. Yeah. You have to cut it with a razor blade. You have to get a table, put it out there, make your measurements. To keep from getting out of line, you have to have them all the same size because it wouldn't look right. And when you put them up, they all in rotation. They hang…

186.t: Putting the pictures away, broken glass and smoking chatter
186.s: She discusses what her husband's picture cost, the glass broken on Medina Street, and says she does not smoke.
186.q: Oh, that's a habit I haven't got. Oh, well you're lucky.

601.t: Amateur baseball in Algiers and the story of the substituted players
601.s: Martin says Yank played on an amateur team whose park was in front of his house. Tom tells a story of a game against the Sweevers where the home side slipped two ringers in, with a mascot who shouted for them.
601.ch: Algiers places, ball games and Frankie Duson
601.q: You take Coach Frankie Duesen out and I don't remember he was four that time.

272.s: He played both Morrison's, one in town and one on the highway.
272.ch: Morrison's, the Slipper and leaving music
272.q: They had one up in town, you see, and one of them out on the highway. You played the one in town? Yeah, I played for one in town. I can remember that one.

303.s: Riddick tells at length how he scratched off a gas-station card and won $100, then tells of meeting William Bendix at Blaise D'Antoni's party.
303.q: It was the funniest thing in the world. And I was down in St. Bernard. I'd been on a call. And I had a brand new car, a Plymouth. And they claimed that if you were out on the road during the first 500 miles, and it came up to 500 miles to add a quart of oil to your car until you could get back to…

308.t: Alley bar and butchers at the market
308.s: Frazier and the interviewer talk about how meat was sold and kept before refrigerators, and how simple life was.
308.q: Right in the alley, you see they had a bar in like a little nightclub, you could call it, right in the back. Like the bar, you come into the alley between the market and the Steinmetz and Ocean's store, and as you come in through that alley like that, you come into, it'd be like a regular bar, you…

155.s: Finley, an insurance man who owned the Kansas City/Oakland team, becomes Budd's friend; stories of Gene Tenace and Finley's health.
155.q: goodness he said the magic word. So he said when you come to New York I’d like to see you and we’ll go to a game together. We became great friends. And one evening, in Chicago, I saw him at an AMA meeting and we went out to dinner together with another doctor. We went to one of these places where…

72.s: A story of a hauling job for a neighbor that netted him almost nothing.
